Preliminary research has explored the alignment of AI with emerging standards, such as ANSI/UL 4600, ISO 21448, and ISO 26262. In the context of ANSI/UL 4600, researchers in [12] define an auditable safety case within the aerospace sector. Similarly, a study on ISO 21448 by [13] highlights the potential necessity of supervisory mechanisms to ensure AI safety. Other studies focus on the ISO 26262 software requirements, proposing adaptations for AI systems [21][22][23][24].

The authors in [15] further identify key safety challenges associated with AI and propose a requirements model, along with an evaluation approach for ensuring conformity. Additionally, numerous works address specific safety challenges introduced by AI, which have been systematically surveyed and categorized at different hierarchical levels by Perez et al. [20]. However, due to the novelty of ISO/IEC TR 5469 and ISO/PAS 8800, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to bridge the gap by proposing compliant architectural designs, an essential step in the development of any safety-critical system.

This paper presents a modular reference architecture pattern for safety-critical EAI systems, addressing the unique challenges of AI integration. Defining a system architecture is a crucial step in safety system development, as it establishes the structural framework, functional interactions, and safety mechanisms necessary to ensure reliability, regulatory compliance, and effective risk mitigation throughout the system lifecycle. By aligning with functional safety and AI standards such as ISO/IEC TR 5469 and ISO/PAS 8800, the proposed architecture bridges the gap between safety and AI by providing a structured framework that integrates safety principles with AI-driven functionalities. The reference safety architecture serves as a reusable foundation, supporting the progressive adoption of EAI in safety-critical domains through an incremental approach. This work introduces multiple safety mechanisms, including diverse redundancy schemes, diagnostic and monitoring mechanisms, and a supervision function, all of which enhance diagnostic coverage and mitigate AI-specific risks, promoting the safe deployment of AI-driven systems. The practical adaptability of the reference architecture is demonstrated through its application to three safety patterns on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin platform. This incremental approach allows experience gained from lower-criticality implementations to improve and refine solutions for higher-criticality applications, fostering a structured and confidence-building transition toward AI integration in safety-critical systems. Although this work does not include a quantitative evaluation of the proposed safety reference architecture, a qualitative assessment has been carried out through review sessions with two independent certification authorities. These reviewers provided expert feedback on the completeness, clarity, and practical relevance of the architectural patterns with respect to safety standards and certification practices. This validation helped shape the architecture to ensure its applicability in real-world safety-critical AI systems. Nevertheless, future work will focus on complementing this with quantitative evaluations to assess the architecture's effectiveness in specific use case instantiations. Therefore, future work will focus on applying the proposed architecture and strategy to specific use cases to validate its effectiveness in real-world safety-critical scenarios. Additionally, further research will be dedicated to developing and evaluating specific safety mechanisms that support the implementation of the proposed safety patterns. This includes assessing their performance and suitability using quantitative metrics such as DC together with fault injection to determine their appropriateness for different SILs. In addition, we acknowledge the critical importance of cybersecurity and its intersection with functional safety, particularly in addressing adversarial threats and model Manuscript submitted to ACM robustness. Integrating security considerations into the proposed architecture is therefore identified as an essential direction for future work.

Integrating EAI into safety-critical systems necessitates adherence to established functional safety standards to ensure these systems operate reliably and safely. Recent advancements have focused on developing frameworks and methodologies to address the unique challenges posed by EAI in this context. Considerable efforts are devoted to standardization frameworks, with new functional safety standards such as ISO/IEC TR 5469 [14], ISO/PAS 8800 [6], ANSI/UL 4600 [4], ISO 21448 [3] and VDE-AR-2842-61 [5] that focus on ensuring AI systems operate safely within their intended contexts. Compliance involves conducting risk analysis, developing a safety plan to mitigate identified risks, and collecting evidence of adherence to the standards. Adhering to these frameworks and practices is essential for organizations aiming to develop and deploy AI in critical systems.
